newsitem.title: USA: Florida man who beat big tobacco is philosophical.
newsitem.headline: Florida man who beat big tobacco is philosophical.

text.p: - Grady Carter, when he isn't playing golf or tinkering with his motorcycle, sometimes makes his way to the Jacksonville courthouse where R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., is defending itself against charges it caused a woman to die of cancer.

He sits quietly in the back of the courtroom, listening to the familiar cadences of tobacco testimony: Cigarettes cause cancer. But people know the risk. Nicotine is addictive. But people quit every day.
He has heard it all before. But what most people have not done is beat the tobacco industry in court.
Carter, 66, did just that last year, in the same courtroom, winning the largest award ever against a tobacco company -- $750,000.
"It was never about the money," Carter said in an interview. "I was just hoping it would be the start of a trend. I wanted the worm to turn on the tobacco companies."

Carter might never have taken on the tobacco industry if he had not been sitting home one day in 1994, part of one lung lost to cancer, listening to cigarette makers tell Congress their product was not addictive.

"I smoked from 1947 to 1972," said Carter, a retired air traffic control manager. "Lucky Strikes. I bought 'em. I smoked 'em. I'm responsible for what happened to me. But when I heard those guys saying they weren't addictive, I just wanted to get a lawyer."
The lawyer he got was Norwood "Woody" Wilner, the same lawyer now pursuing R.J. Reynolds on behalf of Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who died of cancer before her case came to trial.
R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
Even if he won, Carter knew he might never see the money. And so far, he has not. Brown & Williamson, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc, is appealing.
"They can't afford to lose," Carter said. "They have to keep fighting. There are too many sick smokers out there who could sue them. Thats OK. I just wanted to expose their fraud and their secrets.
"Hundreds of people die every day from smoking and you can't say the tobacco companies have no responsibility."

The Carter jury's judgment against Brown & Williamson caught industry analysts by surprise. Even after the dust settled and the crippled tobacco stocks corrected themselves, analysts were saying the Carter judgment was a fluke.
If they win again, Carter said, no one will say so any more.
His life has returned to normal. His cancer has been in remission for six years. He plays golf three times a week and takes vacations with his wife, Millie. He is philosophical about his victory.

"We showed other people that you can take them on," Carter said. "But no one will ever put the tobacco companies out of business. They have too many addicts out there who need them. I know. I was one of them."
